whyNot.C: Full device encryption covers only the encryption requirement.
whyNot.D: Removing administrative rights limits user actions but provides none of the listed management features.

71.why: The iexplore.exe source and target MD5 hashes differ, indicating the file was altered, so a file integrity check should be reviewed.

whyNot.A: A web application firewall protects web servers and does not explain a modified local executable.
whyNot.C: Data execution prevention blocks code execution in memory regions and does not show the hash mismatch.
whyNot.D: Removable media control is not indicated, since USB.exe hashes match and its status is stopped.

72.why: A domain administrator is a privileged user account in the directory, so the administrator is using a user account with elevated rights.

whyNot.A: A guest account has minimal privileges and cannot restore a domain controller.
whyNot.B: A service account runs applications or services, not a person performing manual recovery.
whyNot.D: A local account exists only on one machine and is not a domain administrator credential.

73.why: A proximity card (something you have), fingerprint (something you are), and PIN (something you know) are three distinct authentication factors.

whyNot.B: Fingerprint and voice recognition are both inherence factors, so only two factor types are used.
whyNot.C: Smart card and both certificates are all something you have, so they are one factor type.
whyNot.D: Smart card and proximity card are both something you have, and voice is the only other factor.

74.why: RADIUS federation lets organizations trust each other's 802.1X authentication, so visiting employees authenticate through their home RADIUS server using the native client.

whyNot.A: Shibboleth is a web SSO federation system and is not used for 802.1X wireless authentication.
whyNot.C: SAML exchanges web authentication assertions and is not supported by native 802.1X supplicants.
whyNot.D: OAuth handles delegated authorization for apps, not network access authentication.
whyNot.E: OpenID Connect is a web authentication layer on OAuth and does not work with native 802.1X clients.

75.why: Error handling means returning generic messages that do not reveal details. This screen discloses that the password mismatches the username and exposes the length requirement, which helps attackers.

whyNot.A: Input validation checks that supplied data is well-formed; the problem here is the content of the error message, not the input.
whyNot.C: Obfuscation hides code logic and does not govern what messages the logon screen displays.
whyNot.D: Data exposure concerns sensitive data stored or transmitted unprotected; the issue here is verbose error output.

76.why: Eliminating shared accounts ties every action to one individual, usage auditing and review records and reports anomalous PHI access, and real-time copying to WORM storage prevents log deletion or modification.

whyNot.B: A naming convention aids organization but does not enforce single-person accountability, recording, or log immutability.
whyNot.D: Account lockout thresholds limit brute-force guessing and do not address auditing or log integrity.
whyNot.F: Time-of-day restrictions limit when access occurs and do not create audit trails or protect logs.
whyNot.G: Permission audits review assigned rights periodically but do not record access or make logs tamper-proof.

77.why: Hardware made before 802.11i (WPA2) supports only WPA with TKIP, which was designed to run on legacy WEP-era hardware via firmware updates.

whyNot.A: CCMP requires AES-capable hardware, which pre-802.11i legacy equipment generally lacks.
whyNot.B: WPA2 is the 802.11i implementation and pairs with CCMP, which legacy devices cannot support.
whyNot.D: WPA2 is not available on pre-802.11i equipment, so this combination would not connect.

78.why: A competitor has a clear motive to steal proprietary information to gain market advantage and shorten its own development time, which is industrial espionage.

whyNot.B: Hacktivists are driven by political or social causes, not by market advantage.
whyNot.C: Insiders may steal data, but the stated goal of market edge and time to market points to a competing business.
whyNot.D: Organized crime seeks direct financial gain such as ransom or resale, not faster product development.

79.why: Vendor diversity avoids reliance on a single vendor's products, so one vendor's vulnerability or failure does not compromise everything, improving resiliency.

whyNot.A: Sustainability concerns long-term environmental or operational viability and is not the security benefit of vendor diversity.
whyNot.B: Homogeneity is the opposite of diversity and creates a single point of failure.
whyNot.D: Configurability refers to adjustable settings and is not a result of using multiple vendors.

80.why: A buffer overflow exploits an interactive process by writing past memory bounds, which can let an attacker execute code and reach restricted areas of the OS.

whyNot.A: Pivoting uses a compromised host to attack other systems on a network rather than exploiting a process to reach restricted OS areas.
whyNot.B: Process affinity binds a process to specific CPUs and is not an attack.
whyNot.D: XSS injects scripts into web pages viewed by other users and does not target OS-level access.

81.why: A rainbow table attack looks up a hash in precomputed tables to find the plaintext, whereas a collision attack finds two different inputs that produce the same hash.

whyNot.B: Rainbow tables recover the original plaintext; they do not use the hash itself as the password (that is pass-the-hash).
whyNot.C: In a collision attack the inputs differ while the hashes match, so hash and input are not equivalent.
whyNot.D: Hash functions are deterministic, so the same input always yields the same hash; collisions involve different inputs.

82.why: The log shows the .hta file was restricted by a default restriction policy while the scan found nothing, indicating application whitelisting blocked the payload from executing.

whyNot.B: The scan reported no detections, so antivirus did not find or quarantine any files.
whyNot.C: The log entry concerns a restriction policy blocking an .hta file, not an update approval process.
whyNot.D: The entries show a real policy block on a suspicious file, not a mistuned SIEM false positive.

83.why: Increased inbound traffic combined with full disks suggests attackers placed unauthorized software, such as malware or file-hosting tools, on the servers.

whyNot.A: Misconfigured devices would not typically explain both rising inbound traffic and filled disk space.
whyNot.B: Log anomalies are symptoms to investigate and not a cause of the disk filling alongside the traffic spike.
whyNot.C: Authentication issues involve failed or abnormal logins and do not explain consumed disk space.

84.why: Sustained 100% CPU use can starve legitimate services, causing a denial of service, and it is itself resource exhaustion of the server's processing capacity.

whyNot.A: A man-in-the-middle attack intercepts traffic and is not caused by high CPU utilization.
whyNot.C: DLL injection is an attacker technique for running code in a process and is not a consequence of CPU load.
whyNot.D: A buffer overflow is a memory-handling flaw and is unrelated to high CPU utilization.

85.why: MD5 is a hashing algorithm, and hashes are used to verify data integrity by detecting changes to the data.

whyNot.A: CBC is a block cipher mode of operation that provides confidentiality, not integrity validation.
whyNot.B: Blowfish is a symmetric encryption cipher used for confidentiality.
whyNot.D: RSA is an asymmetric algorithm used for encryption and signatures, and is not itself a hash for integrity checking.

86.why: Untrusted host errors on a web-based VPN typically indicate the server's certificate has expired, so the browser cannot validate it, especially after an unused period like holidays.

whyNot.B: An unsupported browser would fail to load the page entirely and not produce an untrusted host error.
whyNot.C: A locked account would give an authentication error after the secure connection is established, not a trust error.
whyNot.D: Reaching a license maximum would produce a capacity or connection-denied message, not an untrusted host warning.

87.why: Infrastructure as a Service gives the customer control over operating systems, storage, and applications, providing the most control among the cloud service models.

whyNot.B: PaaS means the provider manages the OS and runtime, leaving the customer less control.
whyNot.C: SaaS delivers a finished application with the least customer control over the underlying systems.
whyNot.D: Virtualization is an enabling technology and not a cloud service model.

88.why: SCP transfers files over SSH, encrypting data in transit and replacing cleartext file transfer such as FTP or TFTP.

whyNot.A: HTTPS secures web traffic and is not the standard protocol for network device file transfers.
whyNot.B: LDAPS secures directory service queries and is not used for file transfer.
whyNot.D: SNMPv3 secures device management and monitoring and does not transfer files.

89.why: For a network incident, traffic captures and logs show what crossed the network and when, making them the most likely evidence to determine what happened.

whyNot.A: Volatile memory capture reflects a single host's state and is less central to analyzing network activity.
whyNot.C: Screenshots capture only a momentary visual view and lack the detail needed to reconstruct a network incident.
whyNot.D: A system image capture preserves a host's disk and is more relevant to host-based incidents than network ones.

90.why: The netcat command (nc) with a listen/connect option and a non-standard port 9856 is what creates an arbitrary socket between hosts. Other history entries are ICMP, traceroute, or process-kill commands.

whyNot.A: traceroute sends probe packets to trace the path to 8.8.8.8 and does not establish a persistent socket to an internal host.
whyNot.B: ping uses ICMP, which has no ports or sockets, and it targeted an external address, not an internal host.
whyNot.D: pskill terminates a process and does not open any network connection.

91.why: SCP encrypts file transfer of both binary and text files over SSH, and certificate-based authentication lets a scheduled script authenticate without an interactive password.

whyNot.A: TOTP is a time-based one-time password, which is unsuitable for unattended scheduled scripts and does not protect file transfer.
whyNot.C: FTP sends data and credentials in cleartext regardless of port, so moving it to a non-standard port does not protect sensitive files.
whyNot.D: SRTP secures real-time voice and video streams, not file uploads.
whyNot.F: SNMPv3 is for secure network device management and monitoring, not for uploading files.

92.why: A hardened host scanned with non-applicable plug-ins or checks yields irrelevant failures, and false positives can report non-compliance that does not actually exist.

whyNot.A: Privileged credentials normally make scans more accurate, so they would not cause many spurious non-compliant findings.
whyNot.C: The incorrect audit file is also a plausible cause of mismatched results, but the key favors plug-in selection and false positives as the best pair.
whyNot.E: A compromised host is possible but less likely than scan misconfiguration, and the question stresses a known hardened host.

92.keyDoubt: C: An incorrect audit file would directly produce many non-compliant results, so it is at least as likely as non-applicable plug-ins, though the key's pair is defensible.

93.why: Sandboxing isolates the application so that exploitation of an unknown vulnerability is contained and cannot easily affect the rest of the system.

whyNot.B: Encryption protects data confidentiality but does not stop an application vulnerability from being exploited.
whyNot.C: Code signing verifies publisher and integrity, not whether the code contains unknown flaws.
whyNot.D: Fuzzing finds vulnerabilities during testing, which is hard to apply to third-party software and does not reduce runtime risk.

94.why: Setting the TTL to 1 means packets expire after one router hop, so traffic cannot be routed to or from the Internet even if firewalls are misconfigured.

whyNot.B: NAT hides internal addressing but is not a security control and can be bypassed by port forwarding or misconfiguration.
whyNot.C: A router ACL is an external control that can itself be misconfigured, which the question rules out.
whyNot.D: Protected ports isolate hosts from each other at layer 2 on a switch and do not block Internet access.

94.keyDoubt: C: A router ACL is the standard, practical way to block Internet access, whereas a TTL of 1 is an unusual host-level setting; though the key's wording about misconfiguration supports TTL.

95.why: Separation of duties splits critical tasks such as creating, modifying, and approving payroll among different people so no one role can complete a fraudulent process alone.

whyNot.A: Least privilege limits access to what a job needs but does not specifically require splitting a process across roles.
whyNot.B: Job rotation moves staff between roles periodically to detect fraud, but does not prevent one role from holding all access.
whyNot.C: Background checks screen candidates before hiring and do not restrict access in a role.

96.why: Pivoting is using a compromised host as a stepping stone to attack other systems deeper inside a network.

whyNot.A: Privilege escalation raises access rights on a system and does not describe moving to other hosts.
whyNot.B: Persistence maintains long-term access to a compromised system rather than launching attacks from it.
whyNot.C: Fingerprinting identifies operating systems and services, which is reconnaissance rather than attack launching.

97.why: The issue recurs only after hours and works during the day, which indicates a time-of-day restriction on the account.

whyNot.A: An expired password would continue to block login the next morning until reset, and it would not clear itself.
whyNot.B: Lacking rights would block access at all times, not only in the evening.
whyNot.D: A lockout would persist or need an unlock, and would not conveniently recur at the same time each evening.

98.why: A host with an IP outside the assigned network sending to the wrong gateway indicates the router interface has the wrong subnet, so the correct subnet must be placed on it.

whyNot.A: A firewall ACL filters traffic and does not fix a subnet or gateway addressing mismatch.
whyNot.C: Changing an access port to a trunk carries VLAN tags and does not correct IP subnet assignment.
whyNot.D: A proxy interface change does not address gateway or subnet misconfiguration.

99.why: Many IoT devices like baby monitors ship with default credentials and settings that owners never change, which lets intruders gain access easily.

whyNot.A: Baby monitors typically cannot run antivirus, so outdated antivirus is not the likely cause.
whyNot.B: Signal strength affects connection quality and range, not whether an intruder can authenticate.
whyNot.C: Social engineering manipulates people, but nothing here suggests the parents were tricked.

100.why: A certificate with a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) lists multiple specific host names, so one certificate can match all three servers' names during the client's host name check.

whyNot.A: A wildcard certificate covers subdomains of one domain, which could also work, but it is less specific and the SAN is the intended answer for named hosts.
whyNot.B: Extended validation proves organizational identity and does not address matching multiple host names.
whyNot.C: Certificate chaining links a certificate to its trust chain and does not make it match multiple host names.

100.keyDoubt: A: If the three servers share a parent domain, a wildcard certificate also satisfies the host name check, so the key is only correct if the names differ.

101.why: Mean time to repair (MTTR) is the average time needed to restore a failed system to operational state.

whyNot.A: MTBF is the average time between failures and measures reliability, not restoration.
whyNot.C: RTO is the target maximum downtime allowed, not the measured time to restore.
whyNot.D: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, not restoration time.

102.why: A penetration test actively exploits the vulnerability to show whether it exists and how much damage could result, which a scan alone cannot show.

whyNot.B: A vulnerability scan detects whether the flaw exists but does not demonstrate the extent of potential harm.
whyNot.C: Active reconnaissance gathers information about targets and does not assess impact.
whyNot.D: A patching assessment report shows patch status but not exploitability or business impact.

102.keyDoubt: B: The CIO mainly wants to know whether the vulnerability exists, which a vulnerability scan answers directly, so the key overreaches unless impact assessment is required.

103.why: TACACS+ and RADIUS are AAA protocols that centralize authentication for network device administrators instead of using local accounts.

whyNot.B: CHAP is a challenge-response authentication method and not a centralized authentication service.
whyNot.C: LDAP is a directory access protocol and is not the typical AAA solution for network device administration.
whyNot.E: MSCHAPv2 is an authentication protocol used within other systems and does not provide centralized management by itself.

104.why: Active/passive clustering keeps a standby system ready to take over on failure, which improves availability.

whyNot.A: Confidentiality concerns preventing unauthorized disclosure, which redundancy does not address.
whyNot.B: Integrity concerns preventing unauthorized modification, which a standby node does not provide.
whyNot.D: Non-repudiation proves who performed an action and is unrelated to failover configuration.

105.why: Cross-site scripting (XSS) injects JavaScript that runs in the victim's browser, so it can manipulate page elements such as an iframe. This makes it a client-side attack.

whyNot.A: Buffer overflow corrupts memory in a vulnerable process and is not a browser-based HTML or JavaScript manipulation.
whyNot.B: MITM intercepts traffic between two parties and does not inject script into a page's iframe.
whyNot.D: SQL injection targets the back-end database through unsanitized queries, not the client browser.

106.why: A PIN is a knowledge factor. Adding it to a smart card (something you have) creates two-factor authentication.

whyNot.A: A token is another something-you-have item, the same factor type as the smart card.
whyNot.B: A proximity badge is also a possession factor, so it adds no new factor category.
whyNot.C: A physical key is a possession factor and does not add a different factor type.

107.why: The payload embeds script-like data and path strings into a variable, which is an attempt to insert malicious data through JavaScript. Of the listed options, this fits best.

whyNot.A: CSRF forges authenticated user requests and does not use a payload like this.
whyNot.B: A buffer overflow needs oversized input that overruns memory, not path strings.
whyNot.C: There is no SQL syntax in the payload, so this is not SQL injection.
whyNot.E: Firewall evasion script is not a standard attack category, and the payload does not fragment or obfuscate traffic.

108.why: Rainbow tables are precomputed hash-to-plaintext lookups that let an attacker recover passwords from stolen hashes quickly. Salting defeats them.

whyNot.A: Iptables is a Linux firewall rule framework, not a password-cracking aid.
whyNot.B: NAT tables map internal and external addresses and have nothing to do with hashes.
whyNot.D: ARP tables map IP addresses to MAC addresses and do not hold password hashes.

109.why: An open network accepts any legacy device, and an SSL VPN then supplies strong encryption and authentication independent of the wireless hardware. That gives security plus backward compatibility.

whyNot.B: WPA with a preshared key uses weaker TKIP-era protection and shares one key among all users.
whyNot.C: WPA2 with 802.1X is strong but may not be supported by older devices, so it fails the compatibility requirement.
whyNot.D: WEP with a 40-bit key is trivially cracked and provides no meaningful security.

110.why: A credentialed scan logs in to the host, so it can inspect internal settings such as file system permissions that an external, non-credentialed scan cannot see.

whyNot.A: OS enumeration can usually be done by fingerprinting without credentials.
whyNot.B: Network footprinting is done externally and does not need credentials.
whyNot.C: Open port and listening service checks are standard non-credentialed scan functions.

111.why: A Certificate Revocation List (CRL) publishes revoked certificates, so every browser and system can be told to distrust the hijacked certificate regardless of browser type.

whyNot.A: SSL is an encryption protocol and provides no way to revoke a compromised certificate.
whyNot.C: PKI is the overall trust framework and is not a specific revocation mechanism.
whyNot.D: An ACL filters access to resources and does not invalidate certificates.

112.why: The unknown winserver.exe holds an established connection to a remote host on port 5000. This indicates a remote access trojan (RAT) giving an attacker control, likely bundled with the freeware.

whyNot.B: A keylogger records keystrokes and does not typically maintain a remote control session like this.
whyNot.C: Spyware collects user information but does not usually provide interactive remote control.
whyNot.D: A worm self-propagates across the network, and the output shows no spreading activity.
whyNot.E: A bot would typically beacon to a C2 server for commands, and this output shows a persistent remote session instead.

113.why: Blocking personal email on corporate systems and restricting social media reduce the channels through which phishing messages and data leakage reach employees. Both shrink the phishing attack surface.

whyNot.A: An additional firewall does not stop users from opening malicious email links or attachments.
whyNot.B: A redundant email server improves availability, not phishing resistance.
whyNot.D: Updating X.509 certificates affects encryption and identity, not the content of phishing messages.
whyNot.F: Reviewing file server access violations looks at internal permissions and does not address the phishing vector.

114.why: After evidence is gathered and secured, eradication and recovery, meaning removing the malware and restoring normal operation, is the next step to limit business impact.

whyNot.A: Identifying the attacking host is investigative work that can wait and does not restore operations.
whyNot.B: The incident response plan has already been engaged, since evidence was gathered under it.
whyNot.C: Lessons learned is the final phase, after recovery.

115.why: Joe broke the company policy requiring a VPN on untrusted networks, and that violation exposed his emails to interception. A policy violation is the root cause.

whyNot.B: Nothing indicates an attacker manipulated Joe into acting, so this is not social engineering.
whyNot.C: Joe acted carelessly rather than with malicious intent, so he is not an insider threat.
whyNot.D: Interception over an open network is a known risk and does not require an unknown vulnerability.

116.why: The script runs on a schedule and deletes the file system if a specific user account is missing from /etc/passwd. That is a logic bomb, code triggered by a condition.

whyNot.B: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software, and this script is a condition-triggered payload.
whyNot.C: A backdoor provides unauthorized access, and this script gives none.
whyNot.D: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment, whereas this script deletes files.
whyNot.E: A rootkit hides its presence at a low level, and this script does no concealment.

117.why: Shredding physically destroys the media, so the data cannot be recovered and the drive cannot be reused.

whyNot.B: Wiping sanitizes the drive but leaves it reusable.
whyNot.C: Low-level formatting leaves the drive reusable and may leave recoverable data.
whyNot.D: Repartitioning only changes the partition table and leaves the data recoverable.
whyNot.E: Overwriting destroys the data but leaves the drive reusable.

118.why: Chain of custody begins by documenting the evidence as received. Updating the evidence log records who has the drive, when, and in what condition before any handling.

whyNot.A: A forensic copy is made after the evidence is logged and secured.
whyNot.B: Hashing verifies integrity but comes after the custody record is started.
whyNot.C: Recovering data is analysis, which comes after custody is documented.

119.why: The manager is still determining scope and facts of the compromise, which is the Identification phase of incident response.

whyNot.A: Recovery restores systems after the threat is removed, which has not happened here.
whyNot.B: Eradication removes the threat, and no removal actions have started.
whyNot.C: Containment isolates affected systems, and no isolation steps are described.

120.why: A cloud-based DR site is geographically independent of the hurricane zone and can be provisioned and failed over automatically, giving continuous availability with the least staff effort.

whyNot.A: A hot site gives fast failover but needs dedicated hardware, upkeep, and staff, so it uses more man hours.
whyNot.B: A warm site needs manual activation, data restoration, and configuration before use, so it is not always operational.
whyNot.C: A cold site has only space and power, so bringing it online takes the most time and effort.

121.why: A domain administrator login is an individual, named user account that has been granted elevated privileges, so it is still a user account type.

whyNot.A: Shared accounts are used by multiple people, but domain admin credentials should belong to one accountable administrator.
whyNot.B: A guest account is a low-privilege, limited-access account and would never hold domain administrator rights.
whyNot.C: A service account is used by applications and services to run processes, not by an administrator performing recovery.

122.why: A trust model, such as cross-certification or bridge trust between the two PKIs, lets each organization's certificates be validated by the other, avoiding certificate errors.

whyNot.B: Stapling attaches OCSP revocation status to a TLS handshake and does not establish trust between separate PKIs.
whyNot.C: An intermediate CA issues certificates beneath one root and does not link two independent PKI hierarchies.
whyNot.D: Key escrow stores copies of private keys for recovery and has no bearing on cross-PKI trust.

123.why: Pass-the-hash abuses captured NTLM password hashes for authentication, so disabling NTLM removes the mechanism the attack relies on and minimizes the risk.

whyNot.A: CHAP is a challenge-response protocol used for PPP and does not address NTLM hash reuse on Windows.
whyNot.C: Enabling Kerberos alone does not help while NTLM remains available as a fallback for the attacker to abuse.
whyNot.D: PAP is a plaintext PPP authentication protocol and is unrelated to pass-the-hash on Windows.

124.why: A fingerprint is something you are, so a handwritten signature adds a behavioral something-you-do characteristic, which differs from the existing physical biometric.

whyNot.A: Facial recognition is another something-you-are physical biometric, so it does not add a distinct factor.
whyNot.C: Palm geometry is also a something-you-are physical biometric and duplicates the fingerprint category.
whyNot.D: Iris recognition is another something-you-are physical biometric and adds no new factor type.

125.why: A vulnerability scanner enumerates software versions, running services, supported cipher suites, and configuration or permission settings, then reports weaknesses based on them.

whyNot.B: A protocol analyzer captures and decodes network traffic and does not audit host permissions or installed versions.
whyNot.C: A network mapper discovers hosts and open ports but does not assess permissions or encryption support in depth.
whyNot.D: A web inspector examines web page elements and traffic and does not produce a broad host assessment report.

126.why: ALE equals SLE times ARO, so at an SLE of $500 and ARO of 5, the ALE is $2,500, which does not exceed the $2,500 control cost.

whyNot.B: An SLE of $1,000 gives an ALE of $5,000, which exceeds the $2,500 cost and justifies buying protection.
whyNot.C: An SLE of $2,000 gives an ALE of $10,000, far above the control cost, so purchase is justified.
whyNot.D: An SLE of $2,500 gives an ALE of $12,500, strongly justifying the protection spend.

127.why: Mobile application management controls which apps managers can install and how they are configured, allowing whitelisting, blacklisting, and update control on company-issued phones.

whyNot.A: A download manager handles file transfers and does not govern which applications may be installed.
whyNot.B: A content manager controls documents and data on the device, not the installation of applications.
whyNot.C: Segmentation manager is not a standard mobile management tool and does not control app installation.

128.why: A sponsored guest account ties each guest's wireless access to an employee sponsor, providing individual accountability and time-limited access for non-employees.

whyNot.A: Shared accounts hide individual identity, which defeats accountability.
whyNot.B: A preshared password is known by everyone, so activity cannot be tied to a specific person.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits permissions but does not provide per-user accountability for wireless access.

129.why: System sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of VMs across business units, consuming cluster resources and leaving unmanaged systems, which matches the audit finding.

whyNot.A: A buffer overflow is a memory-handling code flaw and is unrelated to cluster resource exhaustion.
whyNot.B: End-of-life systems lack vendor support, but nothing indicates the VMs are unsupported.
whyNot.D: Weak configuration concerns insecure settings, not running out of compute resources from too many VMs.

130.why: The hash in the patch system matches the malicious file, so the package was already malicious when the patch manager downloaded it and then pushed it out.

whyNot.A: The hash recorded in the patch system matches the malware, so corruption after leaving the system did not occur.
whyNot.C: Application whitelist approval does not explain why the patch system itself held a malware-matching hash.
whyNot.D: A logic bomb triggers on a condition and does not explain a matching malicious hash at download.

131.why: Symmetric algorithms such as AES are fast and efficient for encrypting large volumes of data, with the shared key exchanged securely between the two users.

whyNot.B: A hash function is one-way and provides integrity, not reversible encryption for transmitting data.
whyNot.C: A digital signature provides authentication and non-repudiation, not bulk data confidentiality.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides meaning without real cryptographic protection and is not suitable for secure transmission.

132.why: A policy requiring annual badge rekeying is a management-defined rule, so it is an administrative control that governs how physical access is handled.

whyNot.A: A physical control is the actual lock, badge reader, or barrier, not the policy requiring rekeying.
whyNot.B: A corrective control repairs damage after an incident, whereas this policy is a routine preventive measure.
whyNot.C: A technical control is implemented through technology such as software or firewalls, not a written policy.

133.why: Hard-coding full paths to each DLL prevents the application from searching attacker-writable directories, which stops a malicious DLL from being loaded in place of the real one.

whyNot.A: Setting each application's DLL individually does not change the search order that attackers exploit.
whyNot.C: Disabling registry DLL access would break normal Windows functionality and does not stop search-order hijacking.
whyNot.D: Renaming DLLs is security through obscurity and would break dependencies without removing the unsafe search path.

134.why: An SSL VPN using certificates can tunnel at Layer 2 in bridged mode, which carries Ethernet frames and keeps client MAC addresses visible across the tunnel.

whyNot.A: Tunnel mode IPsec encapsulates IP packets at Layer 3, so client MAC addresses are not carried across.
whyNot.B: Transport mode IPsec protects only the payload between hosts and does not carry Layer 2 information.
whyNot.C: L2TP alone provides no encryption or certificate-based mutual authentication and normally depends on IPsec.

135.why: Input validation checks and rejects malformed or unexpected data at the web form before the application processes it, which blocks injection and malformed-input attacks.

whyNot.B: A proxy server filters and caches traffic but does not enforce the application's own data format rules.
whyNot.C: Stress testing measures performance under load and does not stop malformed input from being processed.
whyNot.D: Encoding protects output rendering, such as against XSS, but does not validate incoming data.

136.why: Recovery restores systems and data to normal operation, and copying user files back after rebuilding the OS is part of that phase.

whyNot.B: Eradication removes the threat, and that work was finished once the OS was rebuilt from original media.
whyNot.C: Containment limits the spread of the incident and happens before rebuilding.
whyNot.D: Identification detects and confirms the incident, which occurs at the start.

137.why: A keylogger records keystrokes, which explains a file of captured URLs, usernames, passwords, and text typed into documents.

whyNot.B: A rootkit hides malicious presence and privileged access but does not by itself record typed content.
whyNot.C: A bot takes remote commands for tasks like DDoS or spam and does not typically log keystrokes.
whyNot.D: A RAT gives remote control but the described keystroke-style output file is the signature of a keylogger.

whyNot.B: A shared key is symmetric and only protects the RADIUS client-server secret, not the credential exchange with the user.
whyNot.C: Elliptic curve is an algorithm family, not a key component that must be provisioned.
whyNot.D: MD5 is a weak hashing algorithm and does not encrypt data in transit.
whyNot.F: DES is an obsolete symmetric cipher with a short key and is not appropriate here.

211.why: Fuzzing sends malformed or random input to running compiled code to expose crashes and flaws, so no source code is required.

whyNot.B: Static review examines source code, which an auditor lacks for proprietary compiled software.
whyNot.C: Code signing verifies publisher and integrity, not the presence of security flaws.
whyNot.D: Regression testing confirms that existing functionality still works after changes, not that the code is free of flaws.

212.why: A sandbox isolates the application so untested code cannot escalate privileges or reach the host system, containing any malicious behavior.

whyNot.A: Sandboxes deliberately restrict access to host resources and storage rather than granting full access.
whyNot.B: Sandboxed code is isolated, and relying on the host's protections instead of its own is not the purpose.
whyNot.D: Sandboxing adds overhead and does not speed up processing or logging.

213.why: SSH (SFTP/SCP), FTPS, and HTTPS each provide encrypted transfer of large files to remote servers without email.

whyNot.A: S/MIME secures email messages, and email is ruled out by the size limit.
whyNot.C: SNMPv3 is for secure network device management, not file distribution.
whyNot.E: SRTP secures real-time voice and video media streams, not file transfer.
whyNot.G: LDAPS secures directory queries and is not a file distribution protocol.

214.why: Identifying critical systems is the BIA element that determines which systems cause losses in revenue, referrals, or reputation when unavailable.

whyNot.A: Mission-essential functions are the business processes themselves, whereas the scenario analyzes the systems whose outage causes loss.
whyNot.B: A single point of failure is a resilience weakness, not the BIA element of impact from a system being down.
whyNot.C: Backup and restoration plans are recovery measures that come after the BIA identifies what matters.

215.why: A keylogger records keystrokes into text files, causing input lag and capturing emails and chats, and it can evade a standard virus scan.

whyNot.A: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and it would not leave text snippets of conversations.
whyNot.B: A rootkit hides malware presence but does not by itself capture and store typed content.
whyNot.C: A backdoor provides remote access and does not by itself record keystrokes into files.

216.why: A passive scan observes traffic or configurations without sending probes, so it identifies vulnerabilities without impacting the system or its data.

whyNot.A: Aggressive scans actively probe and can disrupt services or alter data.
whyNot.C: Non-credentialed scans describe access level and still send active probes that may affect the system.
whyNot.D: A compliance scan checks against a policy baseline and does not describe the non-impact approach.

217.why: RADIUS federation authenticates devices or users at the network edge through 802.1X before any captive portal login is presented.

whyNot.A: L2TP is a tunneling protocol and MAC filtering is easily spoofed, so neither provides proper pre-portal authentication.
whyNot.B: EAP-TTLS is an authentication method that needs a RADIUS backend and does not provide the federated device authentication described.
whyNot.C: WPA2-CCMP with PSK uses one shared passphrase and does not authenticate individual devices.

218.why: A compromised IoT camera taking part in an attack on a third-party site is a bot in a botnet, used for DDoS.

whyNot.B: A RAT gives an attacker interactive remote control, but the scenario describes attack traffic against another site.
whyNot.C: A Trojan is malware disguised as legitimate software, which describes the delivery method, not the participation in the attack.
whyNot.D: A backdoor is just a hidden access path and does not explain the coordinated attack traffic.

219.why: Remote wipe through the mobile device manager erases the data immediately, protecting it even though the device is out of the owner's hands.

whyNot.A: Encrypting data requires access to the device, which is already missing.
whyNot.C: Reporting to authorities may help recovery but does not protect the data on the device.
whyNot.D: Changing a password does not remove data stored locally on the device.

220.why: A memory leak steadily consumes private bytes until the pool is exhausted, forcing the application pool to recycle and hurting availability.

whyNot.A: An integer overflow produces wrong values or crashes at a specific operation, not steady memory exhaustion.
whyNot.B: A buffer overflow overwrites adjacent memory and does not gradually consume private bytes.
whyNot.C: A race condition arises from timing between threads and does not cause progressive memory consumption.

221.why: Rule-based access control enforces predefined rules in the ACL, and the rules grant User3 only Audit, so the write request is denied.

whyNot.B: Mandatory access control relies on classification labels and clearances, which are not shown here.
whyNot.C: Discretionary access control lets resource owners grant access at their discretion, which is not what is shown.
whyNot.D: RBAC assigns permissions by job role, but the denial here comes from the explicit ACL rules.

222.why: Incremental backups copy only changes since the last backup, so they run faster, while differential backups copy everything changed since the last full backup.

whyNot.A: The two types differ in what they copy, not just when they run.
whyNot.B: Differentials grow larger each day and take longer to back up than incrementals.
whyNot.D: Incrementals back up data since the last backup of any type, not since the last differential.
whyNot.E: Differentials restore faster because only the full backup plus the latest differential are needed.

223.why: Application whitelisting allows only approved programs to run, which blocks unknown malware on legacy systems even when AV signatures miss it.

whyNot.A: Blacklisting blocks only known-bad applications, which is the same limitation that lets the malware slip past AV.
whyNot.C: Blockchain analysis is unrelated to preventing malware execution on workstations.
whyNot.D: ACLs control access to resources and do not stop unauthorized executables from running.

224.why: A worm self-replicates and spreads across the network without user action, which produces the repeated propagation pattern an IDS flags.

whyNot.A: A Trojan relies on user execution and does not self-propagate across hosts.
whyNot.B: A bot generates command-and-control and attack traffic, not self-propagating scanning.
whyNot.C: A logic bomb triggers on a condition and does not spread over the network.

225.why: Banner grabbing connects to a service and reads the identifying banner it returns. Nmap (service/version detection), Netcat, and Telnet can all open a connection to a port such as 80 and show the Apache banner.

whyNot.A: Arp displays or manipulates the IP-to-MAC address cache and never queries a service banner.
whyNot.B: Tracert maps the hop-by-hop network path to a host and does not read service banners.
whyNot.F: Grep searches text for patterns and cannot connect to a remote service.
whyNot.G: Nslookup queries DNS records and does not retrieve banners from a web server.
whyNot.H: Netstat lists local connections and listening ports but does not probe remote services for banners.
